bases.name: Stock
bases.notes: Chicken or veg cube. Use chicken for meat dishes, veg for fish or vegetarian.

bases.name: Light coconut milk
bases.sw_note: ~2.5 syns per 100ml light — one tin split 5 ways is manageable

aromatics.name: Onion + garlic
aromatics.notes: Base of every sauce. Always start here.

aromatics.name: Ginger
aromatics.notes: Add for Asian and Indian. Keeps 3 weeks in the fridge.

aromatics.name: Lemongrass paste
aromatics.notes: Tube — keeps forever. Thai and Vietnamese.

spice_profiles.name: Indian
spice_profiles.spices: 1 tsp cumin + 1 tsp ground coriander + 0.5 tsp turmeric + 1 tsp garam masala

spice_profiles.name: North African / Middle Eastern
spice_profiles.spices: 1 tsp cumin + 1 tsp ground coriander + 0.5 tsp cinnamon + 1 tsp paprika

depth.name: Tomato paste
depth.notes: Adds body and richness. Use in all tomato-based sauces.

depth.name: Worcestershire sauce
depth.notes: Good in any tomato-based sauce and in the French-style.

depth.name: Soy sauce
depth.notes: Asian sauces. Light soy for delicate dishes, dark for richer ones.

depth.name: Fish sauce
depth.notes: Very strong. Easy to overdo. Thai and Vietnamese. Can also sneak 1 tsp into Italian for depth.

depth.name: White miso
depth.sw_note: Check brand — typically 1-2 syns per tbsp. Keeps months in the fridge.
depth.notes: Japanese, Chinese, Korean. Also works as a general umami booster in stocks.

depth.name: Peanut butter
depth.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp — 2 tbsp split 5 ways is about 1.2 syns each
depth.notes: West African and Thai. Use smooth. Thickens the sauce naturally.

fresh_herbs.name: Coriander
fresh_herbs.use: Stir in at end or scatter as garnish. Never cook it.

fresh_herbs.name: Italian herbs
fresh_herbs.use: Fresh basil stirred in at end. Dried oregano or dried basil can go in earlier.

fresh_herbs.name: Flat-leaf parsley
fresh_herbs.use: Stirred in at end or garnish.

thickener.name: Thickening granules
thickener.notes: Add at end to any stock-based sauce — stir in gradually until you reach the consistency you want. Not needed for tomato-based sauces which reduce naturally in the oven. Check SW syn value on your brand but typically negligible per portion.

dressing_extras.name: Capers
dressing_extras.notes: Jar — keeps for months. Briny and punchy. Use straight from the jar, no prep.

dressing_extras.name: Dijon mustard
dressing_extras.notes: Emulsifies dressings so they don't split. Adds mild heat without affecting kids.

dressing_extras.name: Balsamic vinegar
dressing_extras.sw_note: ~1 syn per tbsp — check brand. Use sparingly.
dressing_extras.notes: Richer and sweeter than red wine vinegar. Good in warmer salads and roasted veg dressings.

dressing_extras.name: Tahini
dressing_extras.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp — worth it split across 5
dressing_extras.notes: Sesame paste. Thickens dressings, adds nuttiness. Middle Eastern and Mediterranean.

sauces.name: Herbed Jus

recipe_5.method: Soften shallots and garlic gently — don't let them colour. Add stock and Worcestershire. Simmer and reduce by about a third. Thicken with granules to your liking. Add lemon and parsley off the heat. Clean and simple — the protein should be the main event here.

elevate.tip: A small glass to deglaze after softening the shallots — reduce by half before adding the stock for complexity and acidity.
Use instead of flat-leaf parsley for a more distinctly French result. The aniseed note is a classic pairing with chicken and fish.

sauces.description: A classic of the French kitchen — the sauce that appears alongside every serious roast. Lighter than a British gravy and more elegant, it's best in autumn and winter when the slow-roasted meats it's built for come into their own.

sauces.name: Sauce Provençale
sauces.description: Southern France on a plate — slow-cooked tomatoes, garlic and herbs from the garrigue. Bright where Herbed Jus is rich, and deeply summery even when made in January with tinned tomatoes. The capers cut through and stop it being just another tomato sauce.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon into the garlic before the tomatoes go in — it dissolves completely and adds a savoury backbone the finished sauce won't taste like.
A small piece, finely chopped and stirred in at the end, gives a brightness that lifts the whole pot.

recipe_5.method: Fry garlic briefly — 60 seconds, don't let it colour. Add tomato paste and stir for a minute. Pour in tomatoes with the thyme and oregano. Simmer uncovered for 25–30 minutes until thickened and dark. Add capers off the heat. Tear in basil just before serving.

sauces.name: French Onion
sauces.description: Soupe à l'oignon reduced to a sauce. Proper caramelisation takes 40 minutes minimum — there are no shortcuts — but what you get is a sweetness and depth that makes a plain chicken breast feel like something worth sitting down for.

elevate.tip: A pinch stirred in at the end gives a glossier, more coating consistency if you want it to cling rather than pool.

recipe_5.method: Cook onions over the lowest heat with a pinch of salt for 40–50 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes. They should be deeply golden and almost jammy — this is where the flavour lives, so don't rush it. Add garlic for the last 5 minutes. Pour in stock, Worcestershire and balsamic. Simmer 15 minutes until reduced by a third. Season.

sauces.name: Pomodoro

ingredients.item: fresh basil, torn (or 1 tsp dried oregano)

recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic in cast iron. Add tomatoes, paste, Worcestershire, vinegar, salt, pepper. Into 180°C oven for 25-30 mins until reduced and slightly caramelised at the edges. Stir in herbs just before serving.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon stirred in at the start — dissolves completely and adds umami depth without any fishy flavour.
Drop a piece in while it oven-braises and remove before serving. Adds a savouriness that's hard to put your finger on.
Add a ladleful of starchy pasta cooking water to the finished sauce before tossing — it loosens the sauce and helps it cling to the pasta properly. Standard practice in every Italian kitchen.

sauces.description: The foundational tomato sauce of Southern Italy — Neapolitan in origin, and younger than it feels, since tomatoes didn't reach Italian kitchens until the 18th century. The simplicity is deliberate: Italian cooking trusts good ingredients over technique, and this is the proof of it.

sauces.name: Salsa Verde
sauces.description: Italy's cold herb sauce — not cooked, not blended smooth, just herbs and sharp things brought together with knife work. Older than chimichurri and arguably more versatile, it lifts anything from a rested steak to a plainly poached fish.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon stirred in adds a deep savoury backbone — you won't taste anchovy, just a richer depth that makes everything else pop.

recipe_5.method: Finely chop parsley by hand for best texture — a processor makes it too wet. Combine with garlic, capers, mustard, vinegar and lemon juice. Taste and adjust: more vinegar for sharpness, more mustard for body. It should be punchy. Thin with a splash of water if needed.

sauces.name: Sofrito

recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic. Add spices and stir for 1 min before adding everything else. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Smokier and earthier than Italian — works particularly well with fish.

elevate.tip: A small glass to deglaze after the aromatics — the alcohol cooks off, leaving a subtle nutty sweetness that's very Spanish.
A pinch bloomed in a tablespoon of hot water, stirred in with the tomatoes. Changes the whole personality of the sauce.
Add a ladleful of starchy pasta cooking water to the finished sauce before tossing — it loosens the sauce and helps it cling to the pasta properly.

sauces.description: The foundation of Spanish cooking — a slowly cooked paste of onions, tomatoes, and garlic that goes into almost everything from paella to stews. Warming and deeply savoury; the patience required is the whole point.

sauces.name: Mojo
sauces.description: From the Canary Islands, not the mainland — the raw, punchy counterpoint to Sofrito's slow warmth. Where Sofrito is built and cooked, mojo is assembled and immediate: garlic, acid, spice. Goes straight on everything.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon in makes this mojo rojo rather than verde — smokier, deeper, with a little heat.

recipe_5.method: Crush garlic with a pinch of salt to a paste. Stir in smoked paprika and cumin, then the vinegar and lemon juice. Fold through coriander. Taste — it wants sharpness and a back note of smoke. Thin with a splash of water if it's too thick. Serve immediately or rest for 30 minutes to let the garlic mellow slightly.

sauces.name: Salsa Roja
sauces.adult_heat_note: Chili flakes or fresh chili at the table

recipe_5.method: Soften onion and garlic. Toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and lime. 180°C oven 25 mins. Stir in coriander at the end. Chili on the table.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon gives smoky, complex heat that goes far beyond chilli flakes — stir in with the tomatoes.
A square of 85% stirred in at the very end. Classic Mexican mole trick — adds depth without tasting chocolatey.

sauces.description: A traditional Mexican sauce built on charred tomatoes and rehydrated dried chillies — the charring technique predates the Spanish conquest and gives it a depth that no amount of cooking time can replicate. Smoky and punchy, equally good warm or at room temperature.

sauces.name: Chimichurri

recipe_5.method: Chop parsley as finely as you can — a food processor works but keep it rough. Combine with garlic, oregano, red wine vinegar, and oil. Season well and rest for at least 20 minutes before serving. Better still, make it a few hours ahead.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon stirred in adds smoky heat — moves it towards Mexican territory but works very well with beef.
A little finely chopped preserved lemon rind in place of some of the vinegar adds salty, citrusy complexity.

sauces.description: Argentina's table sauce — made in bulk for every asado and used as liberally as ketchup. Bright, sharp, and herby, it cuts through fatty grilled meat in a way nothing else quite does. A proper summer sauce.

sauces.name: Tagine Base

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics, toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and paste. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. The cinnamon is what makes this — don't skip it. Stir in herbs at end.

elevate.tip: A quarter, rind only, finely sliced and stirred in at the end. Adds a briny, intensely lemony note that transforms the whole sauce.
A teaspoon stirred through for adults — adds heat and a roasted pepper complexity. Also excellent kept at the table.

sauces.description: The base of Moroccan tagine cooking — a warmly spiced braise that cooks low and slow alongside lamb, chicken, or root vegetables. The combination of sweet spices with savoury meat is distinctly North African, and it's at its best on a cold evening.

sauces.name: Chermoula
sauces.sw_note: Oil-based — roughly 3 syns per portion depending on how generously you dress.

recipe_5.method: Blitz everything to a rough paste — texture is good, it shouldn't be completely smooth. Adjust lemon and seasoning. Use immediately as a sauce or leave overnight as a marinade; it improves with time.

elevate.tip: A small amount of finely chopped preserved lemon rind instead of fresh lemon completely transforms it — more depth, less sharpness.
Stir in a teaspoon for heat and complexity — the standard Moroccan combination and very good on fish.

sauces.description: Morocco's herb sauce and marinade — used across North Africa wherever grilled fish or meat appears. Vibrant green, sharp from the lemon and warm from the cumin. Works particularly well in spring and summer when you want something fresh that still has backbone.

sauces.name: Zhug
sauces.description: Yemen's answer to chimichurri — a raw, electric green sauce that Israel has adopted as its own. Fiercely herbed, faintly spiced, and best made just before serving. Goes on everything from eggs to grilled lamb.
sauces.adult_heat_note: Stir in 1–2 tsp chipotle paste for proper heat — zhug is traditionally built around fresh green chillies, and this brings it back closer to the original.

elevate.tip: 1–2 tsp stirred in adds the chilli fire that zhug traditionally relies on. Start with 1 tsp and taste.
A small piece, finely chopped, adds a fermented citrus note that lifts the whole sauce.

recipe_5.method: Blitz everything in a small processor or chop by hand until you have a coarse, vivid green paste. It should be thick — not a smooth purée. Taste: it wants to be sharp and herby. Adjust lemon and seasoning. Best made fresh; keeps in the fridge for 2–3 days.

sauces.name: Groundnut Stew
sauces.sw_note: 2-3 tbsp peanut butter split 5 ways — roughly 1-2 syns per portion

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics, toast spices 1 min. Add tomatoes and peanut butter — stir well to combine before putting in the oven. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Thickens naturally from the peanut butter.

elevate.tip: One whole pepper in the stew for the last 15 minutes, removed before serving — infuses flavour without the full hit of heat.
A teaspoon of dried ground crayfish (from African food shops) adds the authentic umami note that defines a real groundnut stew.

sauces.description: One of West Africa's great comfort foods — a thick, peanut-based stew that appears in various forms across Ghana, Senegal, and Nigeria. Deeply warming and filling, it improves the longer it cooks.

sauces.name: Masala

recipe_5.method: Soften onion, garlic, ginger. Add spices, toast 1 min. Add tomatoes and paste. 180°C oven 25-30 mins. Stir in lime juice and coriander at the end.

elevate.tip: Replace half the paprika with this for a deep red colour and a mild, complex heat that's very different from regular chilli.
A teaspoon of dried fenugreek, rubbed between your palms and stirred in at the end. The secret finishing touch in every restaurant-quality curry.

sauces.description: The building block of North Indian cooking — an onion, tomato, and spice base refined over centuries and made globally familiar through the British curry house. Warm and aromatic, it works year-round but feels most at home on an autumn or winter evening.

sauces.name: Coconut & Lime
sauces.sw_note: Light coconut milk ~2.5 syns per 100ml — one tin (400ml) across 5 portions
sauces.adult_heat_note: Chili oil or fresh chili at the table

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics with lemongrass paste. Add coconut milk and fish sauce. Simmer gently 15-20 mins — don't boil hard or the coconut milk splits. Add protein with enough time to cook through. Stir in lime juice and coriander at the very end. Fish sauce is strong — taste before adding more.

elevate.tip: 2–3 torn leaves added with the coconut milk, removed before serving. Adds the aromatic citrus note that defines Thai cooking.
Use instead of (or alongside) regular coriander at the very end — aniseed-forward and quite different. Very authentic.

sauces.description: A simplified Thai coconut sauce, lighter than the restaurant versions and brighter from the lime. Built on Thailand's four-way balance of sweet, sour, salty, and heat — fresh enough for summer but warming enough to work into autumn.

sauces.name: Lemongrass Broth
sauces.adult_heat_note: Fresh chilli or chilli oil at the table

recipe_5.method: Gently soften onion and garlic. Add lemongrass paste and cook 1 min. Add stock and fish sauce — taste before adding more, it's very salty. Simmer 15 mins below a boil. Add lime juice and coriander off the heat. Lighter than Thai with no coconut milk — clean, fragrant and very good with fish and prawns.

elevate.tip: One or two simmered in the stock and removed before serving — adds the aromatic backbone of a proper pho.
A teaspoon alongside the lime juice adds another layer of acidity and a slightly different brightness.

sauces.description: Vietnamese cooking is often described as the freshest of the Southeast Asian cuisines — more herbs, more citrus, less fat. This broth follows that logic: light, fragrant, and built for poaching rather than coating.

sauces.name: Rendang Base
sauces.description: Malaysia and Indonesia's slow-braised masterpiece — a sauce that cooks down until it almost fries in its own aromatics. Where Thai curries stay bright and fresh, rendang goes dark and complex: earthy from turmeric, warm from cinnamon, deeply layered from the long slow simmer.
sauces.sw_note: Light coconut milk keeps this lower — roughly 3 syns per portion. Use half a tin topped up with stock to reduce further.

elevate.tip: 2–3 leaves simmered in add the citrus note that's distinctly Southeast Asian — hard to replicate any other way.
Half a teaspoon, toasted and added with the dry spices, adds an anise depth found in some regional rendang variations.

recipe_5.method: Fry lemongrass paste, garlic and ginger for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and starting to stick. Add dry spices and stir for a minute. Pour in coconut milk. Simmer on a low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the sauce darkens and thickens. For a proper rendang effect, keep going until the coconut milk separates and the paste begins to fry — another 10–15 minutes.

sauces.name: Satay
sauces.sw_note: Peanut butter and sesame oil both synned — roughly 4–5 syns per portion.

recipe_5.method: Whisk peanut butter, soy, lime juice, sesame oil, ginger, and garlic together. Add warm water a tablespoon at a time until pourable. Taste and adjust — more lime for sharpness, more soy for salt. It thickens when it cools, so loosen again before serving.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon added to the mix brings heat and a fermented depth — more Korean-leaning but very good.
Finely shredded and stirred in just before serving for a bright citrus fragrance.

sauces.description: Southeast Asian in origin, with roots in Indonesian and Malaysian street food — the sauce that arrives with skewers of grilled meat at every night market from Jakarta to Kuala Lumpur. Rich and nutty, with enough lime and soy to stop it being heavy. Works year-round.

sauces.name: Five Spice Wok
sauces.sw_note: Miso is synned — check brand. Soy sauce is free.

recipe_5.method: High heat throughout. Stir-fry aromatics until just softening. Add five spice, toss 30 secs. Add stock, soy, miso, vinegar. Cook protein and veg in the sauce. Thicken with granules at the end.

elevate.tip: A splash into the hot wok before the stock — adds the characteristic flavour that separates restaurant Chinese cooking from home versions.
A tablespoon stirred in adds glossy, savoury depth. Worth keeping in the fridge — it lasts months and transforms stir-fries.

sauces.description: A Chinese stir-fry sauce built around five spice — the ancient blend of star anise, cloves, cinnamon, Sichuan pepper, and fennel that sits at the heart of Chinese cooking. Fast and bold; needs a hot pan and a short clock.

sauces.name: Shiro Miso

recipe_5.method: Gently warm stock with garlic and ginger — keep it below a boil. Whisk miso in off the heat or on very low (boiling degrades it). Add soy and vinegar. Taste as you go — it's delicate. Thicken lightly with granules. Garnish with spring onion.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon adds a subtle, clean sweetness that rounds out the saltiness of the miso and soy — don't use more or it tips too sweet.
Replace the stock cube with instant dashi for a more authentic Japanese flavour base. Huge difference for very little effort.
Add a ladleful of starchy pasta cooking water to the finished sauce before tossing — it loosens the sauce and helps it cling to the pasta properly.

sauces.description: Shiro miso — white miso — is the mildest and sweetest of Japan's fermented soybean pastes, associated with the refined cooking of Kyoto. Subtle and umami-rich, it works particularly well on delicate fish and autumn vegetables.

sauces.name: Soy & Miso
sauces.sw_note: Miso synned. Gochujang for adults is low-syn — check brand.
sauces.adult_heat_note: Gochujang paste on the side — also doubles as a table chili sauce for Mexican and Chinese

ingredients.item: few drops sesame oil to finish (synned)

recipe_5.method: Soften aromatics. Add stock, soy, miso, vinegar. Simmer 10-15 mins. Thicken with granules. Finish with just a few drops of sesame oil — it's very strong, don't overdo it. Adults add gochujang at the table.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon for adults — the fermented chilli paste that defines Korean cooking. Stir in at the end or keep at the table.
A teaspoon adds subtle sweetness and gloss. The combination of miso, soy and mirin is the foundation of Korean and Japanese sauces.

sauces.description: Korean cooking is built on fermented, bold flavours — doenjang and soy sauce are foundational. This sauce follows that tradition: deeply savoury with enough sweetness to caramelise under heat, and built for the colder months.

rubs.name: Lemon + Thyme

recipe_5.method: Mix and press into meat. Simple and clean — lets the protein do the work. Good on fish fillets in the oven or chicken with roasted potatoes.

elevate.tip: A few sprigs of fresh instead of dried — the difference in aroma is significant. Worth keeping a small pot on the windowsill.
A teaspoon mixed in acts as a binder and adds a gentle sharpness that works particularly well with chicken and fish.

rubs.description: The herb rub of Provence — thyme grows wild across the south of France, and with lemon and garlic it's become the default seasoning for chicken and fish throughout French cooking. Bright and fresh, and at its best in spring and summer.

rubs.name: Erbe

recipe_5.method: Mix and press into the meat. Leave 15 mins if you have time, cook straight away if not. Air fryer at 190°C for 20-25 mins for chicken thighs. Works brilliantly tossed through pasta with roasted veg — no sauce needed.

elevate.tip: A pinch, lightly crushed and added to the rub — particularly good with pork and sausage. Very Italian.
A small smear rubbed into the meat under the herbs before they go on. Disappears completely but adds remarkable depth.

rubs.description: An Italian dry herb rub built around fennel seed and rosemary — the combination that flavours everything from Italian sausage to porchetta. Traditional and straightforwardly rustic, best on pork and lamb in any season.

rubs.name: Adobo
rubs.adult_heat_note: Chili flakes mixed into adults' portion after cooking

recipe_5.method: Mix and coat. Air fryer or griddle pan. Good on chicken thighs sliced and served in wraps or over rice with lime and coriander.

elevate.tip: Replace or supplement the smoked paprika for a deeper, more complex smokiness with subtle heat.
The juice and zest of half an orange in the mix adds brightness and sweetness — particularly good with chicken.

rubs.description: A dry take on the Mexican adobo — traditionally a marinade of dried chillies, vinegar, and spices used to preserve and flavour meat. Smoky, earthy, and warm, it comes into its own over a summer grill.

rubs.name: Jerk
rubs.adult_heat_note: This is already the mild version — adults can add hot sauce

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste. Coat chicken thoroughly — score the meat if thighs so it gets in. Ideally marinate 1hr+. Air fryer at 190°C for 25 mins or oven at 200°C. The allspice is the key flavour — don't substitute.

elevate.tip: Blend one into the marinade for adults — this is the defining heat of proper jerk and really cannot be substituted.
A tablespoon in the wet marinade. Make sure the marinating time is long enough for the alcohol to work into the meat.

rubs.description: Jerk is Jamaican in origin and one of the Caribbean's most distinctive culinary traditions — slow-smoked over pimento wood and seasoned with allspice and scotch bonnet. The dry rub version brings those bold, hot flavours to any grill; a summer rub if there ever was one.

rubs.name: Baharat

recipe_5.method: Mix into a rough paste with the lemon juice. Coat the meat. Oven or air fryer. The lemon juice helps it stick and caramelises nicely. Serve with couscous and scatter fresh coriander or parsley over.

elevate.tip: Finely grated rind mixed into the rub instead of (or alongside) fresh lemon juice — more concentrated and aromatic.
A teaspoon in the rub or scattered over after cooking — adds a herbaceous, sesame note that bridges North African and Middle Eastern.

rubs.description: Baharat simply means 'spices' in Arabic, and every family and region across the Middle East has their own version. This one is warm and aromatic — cumin, coriander, allspice, cinnamon — and suits slow-cooked autumn and winter dishes, particularly lamb.

rubs.name: Berbere

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste with the lemon juice. More complex than any single-cuisine rub — go gently until you know it. Particularly good on lamb shoulder or chicken thighs. Oven or air fryer at 190°C. The allspice is what makes it Ethiopian rather than North African.

elevate.tip: A tiny pinch, lightly toasted and ground — adds a slightly bitter, maple-like note that's a classic berbere ingredient.
A teaspoon in the paste helps caramelisation and tempers the spice complexity — particularly good on chicken.

rubs.description: The spice blend at the heart of Ethiopian cooking — used in doro wat, tibs, and most of the country's slow-cooked stews. More complex than most blends, with fenugreek adding a bitterness that no other cuisine quite replicates, and built for slow cooking on cold nights.

rubs.name: Tandoori

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste with lime juice. Coat chicken and leave at least 20 mins — an hour in the fridge is better. Air fryer or oven at 200°C. The turmeric will colour the meat golden.

elevate.tip: Replace all the paprika with this for the deep red-orange colour and gentle, complex heat of an authentic tandoori.
Half a teaspoon rubbed between your palms and mixed in — dried fenugreek is the ingredient that makes tandoori taste like tandoori.

rubs.description: The tandoor is a clay oven that's been central to Punjabi cooking for thousands of years — this spice paste replicates its effects under a domestic grill. Traditional, North Indian, and at its best in summer when you can finish it over coals.

rubs.name: Ginger Soy

recipe_5.method: Mix and coat. Marinate at least 20 mins — longer is better. The soy acts as a brine as well as a flavouring. Air fryer, griddle, or oven. Good on salmon fillets or chicken thighs over rice.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon in the marinade adds gloss and subtle sweetness that helps caramelisation — the key to a proper teriyaki finish.
A few drops only — extremely strong, but adds the nutty finish that characterises Japanese and Korean cooking.

rubs.description: Not tied to one tradition — ginger and soy feature across Chinese, Japanese, and Korean cooking, and this rub draws from all three. Simple and versatile, it works on fish, chicken, or tofu in any season.

rubs.name: Korean BBQ
rubs.description: The marinade that underpins Korean BBQ without the gochujang heat — soy, sesame, garlic and ginger in proportions Korean cooks settled on long before fusion made them fashionable. Garlic caramelises beautifully over high heat; the sesame comes through as the meat rests.
rubs.sw_note: Sesame oil is synned — use half a teaspoon to bring it to around 1 syn per portion.

elevate.tip: 1 tbsp stirred in adds fermented heat and the sweet-spicy depth that makes Korean BBQ distinctly Korean.
1 tbsp for a cleaner sweetness — more authentic than adding nothing, and it helps the marinade caramelise better.

recipe_5.method: Combine everything and mix well. Coat meat or tofu thoroughly and leave for at least 30 minutes — overnight is better. Cook over high heat for good caramelisation; the marinade scorches quickly so keep it moving or use a very hot grill.

rubs.name: Char Siu

recipe_5.method: Mix into a paste. Score pork or chicken deeply and work the marinade in — at least 1 hour, overnight is better. The five spice and soy should form a red-brown glaze after cooking. Air fryer or oven at 200°C, basting with leftover marinade halfway through.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon in the marinade adds the glossy sweetness that defines restaurant char siu — a small jar lasts months.
A teaspoon adds gentle acidity that balances the soy and helps the glaze caramelise evenly.

rubs.description: Char siu means 'fork roasted' in Cantonese — named for the way strips of pork were traditionally suspended over fire. The sweet, sticky glaze caramelises into the lacquered crust you see in Chinese BBQ shops, and it's one of the great things to do with pork belly.

rubs.name: Miso Glaze
rubs.description: Miso used as a rub rather than a soup base — the natural sugars caramelise under heat in a way nothing else quite matches. Japanese cooks have been pressing it into fish and aubergine for centuries. It brings a quiet, deep savouriness that doesn't announce itself.
rubs.sw_note: Sesame oil is synned — a small amount goes a long way, roughly 1 syn per portion.

elevate.tip: 1 tbsp added to the paste makes it sweeter and more yielding — closer to the dengaku-style glaze used on grilled tofu and aubergine.

recipe_5.method: Mix into a smooth paste. Press generously onto fish, chicken or veg — it should be a thick coating, not a thin glaze. Leave for at least 1 hour; longer for chicken. Cook under a hot grill or in a very hot pan, watching carefully — the miso sugars catch fast and the line between caramelised and burnt is narrow.

dressings.name: Balsamic + Dijon
dressings.sw_note: Balsamic ~1 syn per tbsp. Keep to 1 tbsp across the whole salad.

recipe_5.method: Whisk together. The Dijon emulsifies it so it coats leaves evenly without oil. Slightly richer than a plain vinegar dressing — good on warm salads or with roasted veg.

elevate.tip: A few drops of the proper thick, syrupy kind instead of regular balsamic — completely different product. A little goes a very long way.
A very finely minced small shallot stirred in — the standard addition to a correct French dressing and worth doing every time.

dressings.description: A dressing that sits between French and Italian — balsamic vinegar from Modena meeting the mustard that defines French vinaigrette. Bold and assertive, it suits the bitter leaves of autumn and winter: rocket, radicchio, chicory.

dressings.name: Dijon Vinaigrette
dressings.notes: Proper vinaigrette without the oil — the Dijon holds it together.

recipe_5.method: Whisk vinegar into Dijon. Add shallot. Toss through leaves just before serving — not before or they'll wilt.

elevate.tip: A very finely minced small shallot is the thing that separates a real French vinaigrette from everything else. This is the correct way to make it.
A few leaves, finely chopped — the defining herb of French salads, particularly good with anything involving chicken.

dressings.description: The vinaigrette that every French cook makes without measuring. The Dijon is there for emulsification as much as flavour — it's what makes the dressing hold together — and it's light and versatile enough for any season.

dressings.name: Italian Herb
dressings.description: The dressing that doesn't need writing down in any Italian kitchen — red wine vinegar, garlic, oregano, a little mustard for body. Sharp and aromatic; works on tomatoes, grilled veg, pasta salads, and anything else that needs a clean hit of acidity.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon whisked in adds depth that makes people ask what you did differently — it disappears completely but the dressing tastes rounder.
1 tbsp, roughly chopped, gives a briny sharpness that takes this into puttanesca territory.

recipe_5.method: Whisk vinegar and mustard together first — the mustard emulsifies the dressing and stops it splitting. Add garlic and oregano. Tear in basil just before serving if using fresh. Taste: it should be sharp and aromatic. Scale back the vinegar slightly if it's too aggressive.

dressings.name: Caper Lemon
dressings.notes: Barely qualifies as a dressing — more of a seasoning. No oil needed.

recipe_5.method: Squeeze lemon over, scatter capers, crack pepper. That's it. Add a little caper brine from the jar if you want extra punch.

elevate.tip: One fillet mashed to a paste — invisible in the dressing but adds a savouriness that makes everything taste more of itself.
A few fronds work beautifully with capers and lemon. Particularly good over poached salmon or a warm potato salad.

dressings.description: A dressing built from Mediterranean pantry staples — capers, lemon, good olive oil. Briny and sharp, it belongs on a summer table alongside grilled fish or roasted courgette.

dressings.name: Lemon Herb

ingredients.item: flat-leaf parsley or fresh coriander, chopped

recipe_5.method: Mix and drizzle. Light and fresh — works anywhere you want brightness without weight.

elevate.tip: A very finely minced small shallot, left to macerate in the lemon juice for 10 minutes — mellows the rawness and adds real depth.
A teaspoon of finely chopped rind instead of (or alongside) fresh lemon — more complex, more aromatic, and very different.

dressings.description: A clean Mediterranean dressing that appears in some form across the whole basin — Greek, Italian, Spanish. Light and fresh, it's a spring and summer dressing that works on everything from grains to grilled chicken.

dressings.name: Lime + Coriander

recipe_5.method: Mix and toss through. Good as a slaw dressing or over a Mexican-style chicken salad. Bright and clean.

elevate.tip: Half a jalapeño, very finely minced and stirred through — adds heat without overpowering. Particularly good in a Mexican slaw.
Half a teaspoon to balance the acidity of the lime. Synned, but a small amount makes a noticeable difference — taste as you go.

dressings.description: The flavour combination that runs through Mexican cooking from the street taco upwards — fresh coriander and sharp lime cutting through rich or fatty food. Bright and summery, but works year-round in slaws and grain bowls.

dressings.name: Tahini Lemon
dressings.sw_note: ~3 syns per tbsp tahini — 1 tbsp across 5 portions is about 0.6 syns each

recipe_5.method: Whisk tahini and lemon together — it'll seize up first, keep going. Add water gradually until it's a pourable consistency. Drizzle over roasted veg or falafel.

elevate.tip: Scattered over the top after drizzling — adds herby, sesame crunch that's particularly good over roasted vegetables or falafel.
A teaspoon drizzled alongside — the sweet-sour contrast with tahini is a classic Middle Eastern combination.

dressings.description: Tahini — ground sesame paste — is central to Levantine cooking, appearing in everything from hummus to falafel to baked fish. Loosened with lemon and water it becomes a dressing that works on almost anything, earthy and nutty in any season.

dressings.name: Nam Jim
dressings.notes: A Thai dipping sauce that doubles as a punchy dressing. Fish sauce is very strong — add gradually.

recipe_5.method: Mix and taste — it should be salty, sour and very fragrant. Fish sauce is the dominant flavour so build slowly. Use as a dressing, dipping sauce or light marinade. Keeps in the fridge for a few days.

elevate.tip: Half a bird's eye finely sliced — the proper version has chilli heat. Keep at the table for adults.
Half a teaspoon dissolved in the lime juice is the classic balance to the fish sauce saltiness.

dressings.description: Nam jim simply means 'dipping sauce' in Thai, and there are dozens of versions — all built on the same four-way balance of fish sauce, lime, palm sugar, and chilli. Fresh, sharp, and bright, it cuts through anything rich or fatty.

dressings.name: Ginger Lime
dressings.notes: Add a few drops of sesame oil if you have syns to spend — transforms it.

recipe_5.method: Mix and drizzle. Works cold over noodles, shredded chicken or raw veg. Punchy — a little goes a long way.

elevate.tip: Just a few drops — very strong, but adds the nutty depth that lifts this from a dressing into something restaurant-quality.
Half a teaspoon dissolved in the lime juice — balances the acidity and adds the subtle complexity that defines Thai dressings.

dressings.description: A lighter take on Asian dressing that leads with lime rather than soy — closer in spirit to Vietnamese and Thai cooking than Chinese or Japanese. Fresh and citrusy, it suits summer eating and works particularly well on noodle salads.

dressings.name: Miso & Ginger
dressings.sw_note: Miso is synned — check brand. Two tablespoons across 5 portions is minimal.

recipe_5.method: Whisk together and thin with water until it pours easily — miso thickens it significantly. Taste for balance: you may want a little more vinegar. Works cold over soba noodles, shredded cabbage, roasted sweet potato or cucumber.

elevate.tip: A few drops transforms this into something restaurant-quality. Extremely strong — less than you think.
A teaspoon instead of some of the water — adds subtle sweetness and makes the dressing glossier.

dressings.description: A dressing with roots in Japanese cooking — the miso and ginger combination associated with Kyoto restaurant salads and popularised worldwide by Japanese-American diners. Earthy and savoury, with more depth than any standard vinaigrette.

snacks.name: Peanut Butter Balls
snacks.description: The gym bag staple that actually tastes good — oats, peanut butter and honey held together by chia seeds. American fitness culture codified into a ball. No baking, no fuss, keeps in the fridge all week.
snacks.sw_note: Oats count as a Healthy Extra B; peanut butter and honey are synned. Around 4–5 syns per portion depending on size.

elevate.tip: Roll the finished balls in coconut before refrigerating — adds texture and a slightly tropical note.

recipe_5.method: Mix everything together until it comes together into a sticky dough — if it's too dry, add a little more honey; too wet, a handful more oats. Roll into balls roughly the size of a walnut (about 20 total). Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before eating. Keeps for a week in the fridge.

snacks.name: Tahini Date Bites
snacks.description: Medjool dates and tahini have been eaten together across the Levant for centuries — one sweet, one bitter, each making the other better. No sugar added because none is needed. Dense, rich and satisfying in a way that processed snacks rarely manage.
snacks.sw_note: Dates are synned due to natural sugar content; tahini is also synned. Around 4–5 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: A few drops worked into the tahini deepens the sesame flavour before you mix everything together.

recipe_5.method: Blitz dates in a food processor until they form a sticky paste. Add tahini, cinnamon and salt and blitz again until combined. Roll into balls, then roll each ball in desiccated coconut to coat. Refrigerate for 30 minutes. Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

snacks.name: Chia Coconut Pudding
snacks.description: Thai coconut desserts are built on exactly this logic — rich coconut milk balanced with something sharp and something sweet. Chia seeds do the work overnight. Effortless to make, impressive to serve, and genuinely filling.
snacks.sw_note: Light coconut milk is synned; honey adds further syns. Around 5–6 syns per portion. Use unsweetened almond milk instead to reduce significantly.

elevate.tip: A small thumb grated in before setting adds a warm, faintly spicy note that makes it feel more complex.
Steep 2 leaves in the warm coconut milk before adding the chia — the citrus fragrance is distinctly Thai.

recipe_5.method: Whisk coconut milk, honey and lime juice together. Stir in chia seeds and mix well — they clump if you don't. Leave for 5 minutes, stir again, then refrigerate overnight or for at least 4 hours. The pudding should be thick and spoonable. Top with fruit if you have it.

snacks.name: Miso Almond Clusters
snacks.description: Japanese convenience stores sell roasted nuts glazed with miso and honey — this is that, made at home. The miso's saltiness stops the honey becoming sickly and the clusters caramelise into something genuinely addictive. Ready in minutes once the nuts cool.
snacks.sw_note: Mixed nuts are synned outside of the Healthy Extra B allowance; honey adds further syns. Around 6 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: A second tiny drizzle over the finished clusters as they cool — the raw sesame aroma stays bright where the cooked version goes deeper.

recipe_5.method: Warm miso, honey and sesame oil in a pan over low heat until they loosen into a glaze — 1 minute. Add nuts and stir to coat thoroughly. Tip onto a lined tray in small clusters and leave to cool completely. They'll harden as they cool. Keeps in a jar for 2 weeks.

snacks.name: Spiced Nuts
snacks.description: Every market in the Middle East sells some version of this — spiced, roasted nuts that sit somewhere between snack and condiment. The honey keeps them together; the cumin and smoked paprika do the work. Excellent with drinks and better the next day.
snacks.sw_note: Nuts are synned outside the Healthy Extra B allowance. Around 6 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: A tablespoon stirred in with the spices adds a dried herb and sesame complexity that's distinctly Levantine.
Half a teaspoon in the honey glaze for a spiced, warm version — adds real heat and colour.

recipe_5.method: Toast nuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3–4 minutes until starting to colour. Add honey and spices and stir for another 2 minutes until coated and caramelised. Tip onto a lined tray, spread out and leave to cool. Season with salt. Store in a jar.

snacks.name: Yogurt Bark
snacks.description: Greek yogurt frozen into a slab — a Mediterranean approach to the problem of wanting something cold and sweet without eating ice cream. The honey and cinnamon do minimal work. Keeps in the freezer and breaks into pieces like rough dark chocolate.
snacks.sw_note: Greek yogurt is free; honey is synned. Around 2–3 syns per portion, making this one of the lower-syn snack options.

elevate.tip: Scattered over the top before freezing — adds texture to the finished bark.
A thin drizzle over the honey layer before freezing adds a sweet-tart depth and a deep red colour.

recipe_5.method: Line a tray or baking sheet with parchment. Spread yogurt in a thin, even layer. Drizzle honey over, scatter nuts and dust with cinnamon. Freeze for at least 3–4 hours until solid. Break into rough pieces directly from the freezer. Store in a bag in the freezer.

snacks.name: Coconut Ginger Bites
snacks.description: Loosely inspired by Indian coconut ladoo — the kind made for festivals and celebrations. No ghee, no sugar, just coconut, honey and fresh ginger with chia to bind. Fresh ginger gives them a warmth that dried doesn't, and makes the whole batch smell like a spice market.
snacks.sw_note: Desiccated coconut and honey are both synned. Around 4 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: Half a teaspoon of ground cardamom stirred in is traditional in ladoo and makes these taste more authentically Indian.

recipe_5.method: Mix all ingredients together until it clumps when pressed — if too dry, add a little more honey. Leave to sit for 10 minutes (the chia absorbs moisture and helps it bind). Roll into balls. Refrigerate for 30 minutes. Keeps for a week in the fridge.

snacks.name: Oat Honey Bars
snacks.description: The American answer to the cereal bar, made without the packaging and the ingredient list you need a degree to parse. Oats, peanut butter, honey — pressed into a tray and refrigerated. Batch-friendly and genuinely filling for the calorie count.
snacks.sw_note: Oats are a Healthy Extra B; peanut butter and honey are synned. Around 5–6 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: A handful pressed into the top of the tray before refrigerating adds texture and a toasted coconut note when you cut them.

recipe_5.method: Warm peanut butter and honey together in a pan over low heat until combined and runny. Remove from heat and stir in oats, chia seeds and cinnamon until fully coated. Press firmly into a lined tray — really press it, or it won't hold together. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Cut into bars and keep refrigerated.

snacks.name: Majoun
snacks.description: A medieval Moroccan confection found in manuscripts like the 13th-century Andalusian cookbook Al-Andalus. Dates, nuts and warm spices ground together into dense, aromatic balls — originally made as a travelling provision and restorative food. The original energy bar, unchanged for 800 years.
snacks.sw_note: Dates, nuts and honey are all synned. Around 5–6 syns per portion of four balls.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon stirred in before rolling adds a floral, perfumed note that is very true to medieval Moroccan cooking.
A pinch of finely ground black pepper was common in historical recipes — it cuts through the sweetness unexpectedly well.

recipe_5.method: Blitz the dates in a food processor until they form a thick paste. Add the nuts, honey, cinnamon, ginger and salt and pulse until the nuts are broken down but still have some texture — you want it rough, not smooth. Roll into balls roughly the size of a walnut (about 20 total), then roll each one in desiccated coconut. Refrigerate for 30 minutes before eating. Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

snacks.name: Tahini Halva Balls
snacks.description: Halva in its oldest form — before it became the crumbly block found in shops — was simply tahini worked with honey until it stiffened into something you could shape by hand. Versions of this appear in Persian and Levantine texts going back over a thousand years. Two ingredients, ancient technique, surprisingly complex result.
snacks.sw_note: Tahini and honey are both synned. Around 4–5 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: Roll the finished balls in sesame seeds for extra crunch and a more pronounced sesame flavour.
A pinch stirred into the mix adds a faintly floral warmth that works beautifully with the sesame.

recipe_5.method: Stir the tahini, honey and salt together in a bowl. It will seize and thicken as you work it — this is what you want. If it is too soft to hold its shape, refrigerate for 15 minutes then try again. Roll into small balls (about 20 total). Refrigerate on a tray for at least 30 minutes until firm. Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge — they firm up further over time.

snacks.name: Nut Laddoo
snacks.description: Laddoo appears in Ayurvedic texts as both food and medicine — the Sushruta Samhita mentions modaka, sweet balls of ground nuts, honey and spices, given for strength and recovery. This no-bake version stays close to those ancient roots: crushed nuts, honey, coconut and cardamom, nothing else. One of the oldest snack forms on earth.
snacks.sw_note: Nuts, honey and coconut are all synned. Around 5–6 syns per portion.

elevate.tip: A teaspoon added with the honey gives a Mughal-era fragrance that elevates the whole thing.
A pinch dissolved in a teaspoon of warm water and stirred in turns them a beautiful gold and adds a gentle floral depth.

recipe_5.method: Blitz the nuts in a food processor until finely ground — stop before they turn to butter, you want a coarse sandy texture. Add the honey, 3 tablespoons of the coconut, cardamom and salt and pulse until it comes together into a dough. Roll into balls roughly the size of a walnut (about 20 total), then roll in the remaining coconut. Refrigerate for 30 minutes. Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.
